Cato’s Letters was one of the most widely read political works of the Founding era. The essays taught Americans to view freedom of speech as  “the great bulwark of liberty.”

That is why John Adams later said the “real American Revolution” began before the war, in the “minds and hearts of the people.” Cato’s Letters helped shape those minds and hearts.

On America's 250th, @PaulMeany2 tells the full story in the Summer 2026 issue of the Free Society:

SCOTUS struck down the effort to limit birthright citizenship, holding that the 14th Amendment guarantees citizenship to nearly all children born on US soil. This will limit executive power and prevent a future president or Congress from undoing the rule, says Cato’s @Thomas_A_Berry.

posts.text:
Reports that OpenAI discussed giving the federal government a 5% stake should concern anyone who wants the US to set the pace in AI, says Cato’s @DeHavenTad. Government ownership blurs the line between referee and market participants, creating political risk for developers, customers, and international partners. 
 
“Washington should strengthen US competitiveness through clear, neutral rules—not by taking equity in the companies it regulates.”
